title: JPG vs PNG vs WebP: which image format to use, and when — cv.cm
description: JPG suits photos, PNG suits sharp graphics and transparency, WebP does both in smaller files. Compare compression, quality, support and when to use AVIF.
h1: JPG vs PNG vs WebP: which image format should you use?
answer: Use JPG for photographs where small files matter and transparency does not. Use PNG for screenshots, logos, text and anything that needs exact pixels or a transparent background. Use WebP when the image goes on a website: it supports both lossy and lossless modes plus transparency, and Google measured lossy WebP files 25–34% smaller than JPG at equal quality. Every current browser displays WebP.

sections.h: The three formats side by side
body: Each format was designed for a different job, and the differences come down to how they compress pixels and what extra features they carry.

sections.h: Lossy vs lossless: the deciding difference
body: Lossy compression (JPG, lossy WebP) throws away detail the eye is unlikely to notice. It works well on photos, where colors change gradually, but it smears hard edges: text and thin lines in a JPG pick up faint halos called ringing or mosquito noise, and blocks of 8×8 pixels can appear at low quality.

Lossless compression (PNG, lossless WebP) stores every pixel exactly. It shrinks large areas of flat color very well, which is why a screenshot can be smaller as PNG than as JPG, but a photo saved as PNG is often 3–5 times larger than a good JPG with no visible benefit.

ul: Each time a JPG is edited and saved again, it is compressed again and loses a little more detail. Keep a lossless master if you will edit repeatedly.
Converting a JPG to PNG does not restore lost detail; it only stores the already-compressed pixels without further loss, in a bigger file.
A JPG quality setting of about 80–90% is a common balance between size and visible artifacts.

body: Google's WebP compression study compared files at equal structural similarity (SSIM). Lossy WebP came out 25–34% smaller than JPG, and Google reports lossless WebP about 26% smaller than PNG. Actual savings depend on the image, the encoder and the quality setting.

A worked example: a 400 KB hero photo saved as JPG would typically land around 265–300 KB as lossy WebP at similar quality. Across a page with twenty images, that difference shortens load time on mobile connections.

body.note: WebP is limited to 16,383 × 16,383 pixels and 8-bit color, so it is not a good archive format for high-resolution or HDR originals. Keep the camera original and export WebP copies for the web.

body: AVIF is a newer format that stores AV1-compressed images in a HEIF-style container. It usually beats WebP on file size for photos, supports 10- and 12-bit color and HDR, and handles transparency. Chrome added support in version 85, Firefox in 93 and Safari in 16.

Its trade-offs are slower encoding, weaker support in older desktop software, and occasional loss of fine texture at very low quality. Many sites serve AVIF first, WebP second and JPG as a fallback using the HTML `<picture>` element.

body: If a form rejects WebP, convert a copy to JPG for photos or PNG for graphics. Nothing is gained by converting a lossy file to a lossless one beyond compatibility.

faq.q: Is PNG higher quality than JPG?
faq.a: PNG is lossless, so it keeps every pixel exactly, while JPG discards some detail. For photos the difference at high JPG quality is usually invisible; for text and sharp edges PNG looks clearly cleaner.

faq.q: Why is my PNG so much bigger than the JPG?
faq.a: Lossless compression cannot discard the fine noise and gradients found in photos, so a photographic PNG is often several times larger. Use JPG or WebP for photos.
Yes. Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Opera have supported it for years, and Safari added it in version 14 in 2020. Some older desktop programs and upload forms still reject it.

faq.q: Does converting PNG to JPG remove transparency?
faq.a: Yes. JPG has no alpha channel, so transparent areas are filled with a solid color, usually white or black. Use WebP or keep PNG if you need transparency.
